summary:
The United Arab Emirates screens gender markers at entry and has refused trans travellers entry on identity grounds repeatedly over the past decade. In 2025 two Israeli trans women were detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

Earlier cases follow the same pattern. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and held for five hours at Dubai International Airport, her passport confiscated, after authorities declined to recognise her gender as legitimate. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe pageant, was stopped at Dubai immigration and interrogated for nine hours before being deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

The legal framework underpinning these encounters explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles, and transgender expression or unconventional appearance frequently results in arrest, confinement or expulsion. Article 412(2) of the federal criminal law imprisons for up to one year and fines up to AED 10,000 any man who disguises himself as woman to enter a women-only space, replacing an earlier broader prohibition on clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex.

Consensual same-sex relations were criminalised in a federal criminal code enacted in early 2022. Article 409(1)(b) carries a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed, and charges can proceed only on the complaint of a spouse or guardian. The UAE recognises no legal gender recognition procedure, does not recognise same-sex marriage, and provides no protection under any law or policy against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics.

Detention carries documented physical risk. Detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people; mistreatment in custody has included beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture; and involuntary medical and psychological treatment, including hormonal therapy and detention for forced psychological treatment, has been imposed in connection with suspected or established same-sex conduct. Gay conversion practices are prohibited by no UAE law or regulation.

Approaching the authorities is itself a documented route to arrest. In December 2013 two Brazilian trans women who called police about prejudice they had witnessed in a nightclub were arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported.

Support infrastructure for a visitor in difficulty does not exist on the ground. No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organisation operates openly anywhere in the country, and sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement against gender nonconformity and same-sex conduct has a long record behind the entry refusals. A 2005 raid on a desert resort in Abu Dhabi arrested 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding'; 12 were found guilty, 11 of them receiving five-year sentences and one a year, and initial reports stated that some were told to accept hormone treatment in exchange for lighter sentences. A 2012 raid broke up a party of 30 men in Dubai, and two Indian men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet received six months each plus deportation.

A Brazilian trans woman detained in the country since September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, accused the consulate of negligence in April 2023, a case illustrating prolonged custody with limited consular recourse.

Public statements by officials leave little room for ambiguity: they have declared there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE'. In June 2023 the pop group Steps refused a Dubai performance over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality.

Censorship extends to trans-specific content. The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' flag; the Arabic children's comic Majid was investigated in 2022 over dialogue using the word مثلي, and in June 2023 Amazon removed 150 search terms including 'lgbtq' and 'pride' from its UAE site under threat of penalties.

The complaint requirement in Article 409 produces uneven exposure: because civil guardianship ends at 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual conduct between adult men, whereas for conduct between women a father, male relative or husband can qualify, leaving prosecution possible where such a complainant comes forward.

The pattern of identity-based entry refusals in the Gulf compares unfavourably with the detention cases themselves, in which foreign nationals were held for hours to days and then expelled rather than charged under the criminal provisions described above.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition. The federal framework contains no procedure by which a person's sex marker can be amended, so identity documents continue to record the sex assigned at birth regardless of a person's lived gender, which is the condition that produced the airport screenings of trans travellers.

Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited circumstances tightly controlled by the state, and no framework for recognition of the resulting personhood appears in the sources. LGBTI organisations cannot register, and no LGBTQI+ advocacy or support body operates openly anywhere in the country; in Dubai no formal LGBTQ organisation or venue exists, and a nightclub that sponsored a night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes and the likelihood of state repression are given as the reasons such organisations and community education cannot be established.

Censorship is a resident-facing constraint as well as a visitor one. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites dealing with dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the words 'gay' or 'sex', which limits access to information about healthcare and rights.

Same-sex conduct between consenting adults remains criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), with a minimum six months' imprisonment and no maximum. Article 409 also reaches unmarried different-sex couples, and the spouse-or-guardian complaint requirement shapes who can trigger a prosecution rather than whether the conduct is illegal.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics exists in any UAE law or policy. Gay conversion practices are neither prohibited nor discouraged by any law or regulation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources conflict on the sentence range under Article 409(1)(b): one country overview states 'up to six months' imprisonment' while the fuller legal coverage states a minimum of six months with no maximum prescribed. Which figure governs under the 2021 law is unresolved here.

No enforcement data for Article 412(2) appears in the inventory. Whether the one-year, AED 10,000 provision has been applied since replacing the broader clothing ban, and how often, is not sourced.

The outcome of the 2025 detention of the two Israeli trans women is not sourced beyond denial of entry and passport confiscation; whether they sought review, compensation or a formal complaint is unknown.

The status of the Brazilian trans woman held since September 2022 is not sourced beyond the April 2023 negligence allegation against the consulate. Release, charge or deportation is unresolved.

Reports that some men convicted in the 2005 Abu Dhabi raid were required to accept hormone treatment in exchange for lighter sentences were described in the source as initial reports, and no confirming record is available here.

Whether a legal gender recognition procedure exists under emirate-level practice rather than federal statute is not addressed by the sources; the inventory states only that none exists.
